user: Hey AI—could use a hand here. Of these six legal moves (g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8), which one puts me in the best shape for the rest of the endgame? I care about final disc count, not just immediate flips.
assistant: **b7.** It locks up the entire 7th rank; if White gets in there first, they’ll flip c7–g7 and you lose that whole edge. The other legal moves either flip fewer stable discs or hand White the initiative to take the rank themselves.

user: Okay, the board’s done and I lost 31-33. Walk me through where I went wrong—after b7, was c8 a mistake? g2 felt strong at the time but White punished me with h1.
assistant:
**The short answer: g2 lost the game, not c8.**

- **g2** is the X-square diagonal to corner **h1**. It may have flipped several discs, but it gave White the exact line (f3–g2) to take h1. Corners are permanent; once White had h1, the entire top row (b1–g1) became unflippable. That ~8-disc swing is your 2-disc loss right there.

- **c8** after b7 wasn’t the killer. Without h8 already, an edge square like c8 usually gets flipped back or wastes a tempo in that sector. It didn’t help, but it wasn’t decisive.

- **b7** itself was correct — it locked the 7th rank as planned.

The endgame rule here: **flipping the most discs in the moment means nothing if the move gifts a corner.** Once White took h1, that edge was gone for good.

user: So what should I have played instead of g2 at that point? My legal moves were b6, a7, c8. Would a7 have been the right call?
assistant:
**a7.**  

It flips the entire left edge (a2–a6), giving you six stable, anchored discs that White can almost never reclaim. That single move likely wins by itself.

- **c8** is decent—it flips the bottom too—but it gains fewer safe discs than a7.  
- **b6** is interior; it doesn’t wall off an edge and leaves more play for White.  
- **g2** was the real killer: it opened the long diagonal to corner h1. Once White took h1, they flipped everything along the h1–b7 line and locked up the whole top row.

So the rule of thumb there was: *take the edge anchored by your corner* (a7 to a1) and leave the X-squares (g2) alone. If you had played a7 and left g2 empty, White would likely have been forced to break on g2 themselves—and you’d have taken h1 instead.

user: One more thing—after I played b7, White went a8. That seemed slow, but it set up a3 later which wrecked my a-file. What was the tactical idea behind a8?
assistant: **a8 was an anchor, not a slow move.** By taking the corner, White gave themselves a permanent, unflippable disc at the end of the a-file. That turned a later **a3** into a lethal swing move: any Black discs on a4–a7 were suddenly sandwiched between a3 and the anchored a8, so they all flipped to White. Without that corner anchor, those discs were safe because there was no White disc on the far side to complete the line. White invested one tempo to turn your entire a-file into a trap.

user: Last one—when I played c8 earlier, it only flipped d8. If a7 was the winning move instead of g2, would c8 have ever been useful later, or was it just a wasted tempo no matter what?
assistant:
**Wasted tempo either way.**

c8 is a **C-square** on the bottom edge. It didn’t anchor anything; once White took the surrounding corners/edge, it flipped back (you can see it ended White in the final position). After **a7**, the winning battle shifts to the top-right and **h8**; the bottom edge is only useful if you can take a corner there, and c8 doesn’t do that.
